with, together with

or ξύν. The precepts of the ancient grammarians about the use of each form have been collected in the Thesaurus vol. 7 p. 1165 1166; if the reading of the manuscripts, however much it fluctuates between the two, is compared with these, we seem to understand only this: that the ancient Attics said ξύν (which in inscriptions is sometimes written XCYN) rather than σύν, but that in later times this spelling fell into such disuse that already in Xenophon no examples of it are found, except that in one or two places it was introduced by scribes in inferior books, just as in some inferior manuscripts of Herodotus, who most certainly used only the form σύν, ξύν is often written, and the same has been introduced into many other writers who used only the form σύν; about this L. Dindorf spoke in the Preface to Xenophon's Anabasis p. VIII of the Oxford edition. The dramatic poets, however, used both forms, as very many verses show whose meter requires either σύν or ξύν, although examples that require σύν are rare (three in Aeschylus, Pr. 521 ὃ ξυναμπέχεις [which you cover together], Sept. 839 ἅδε ξυναυλία [this joint music], Ag. 144 τερπνὰ ξύμβολά [pleasing omens]), while very many require σύν in the plays of the three tragedians. It is asked therefore which form should be assigned to the hundred other verses whose meter allows either: in these the inconsistency of the manuscripts is so great, and not rarely there is disagreement among them, that when all the examples are collected nothing else is established except that the scribes wrote now σύν now ξύν at random, and sometimes even with a metrical fault, except that, as Ellendt observed, at the beginning of a senarius in Sophocles in the Medicean codex ξύν is found almost constantly, and indeed the simple ξύν at El. 273 956 1122 1168. Tr.
